brief.text: This piece looks at how networks of neurons, in brains or in AI, can represent many different things using only a few neurons. People often use one phrase, "distributed representations," for two different tricks: combining separate features together (composition), and packing many things into the same neurons at once (superposition).
Telling these two tricks apart matters because they work very differently, and because understanding how a network stores information is key to figuring out how it actually works inside.

Composition builds many combinations, like colors and shapes, out of a few simple features, and is easy to understand piece by piece. Superposition crams more things into fewer neurons than you'd expect, but makes it much harder to read out what's stored. The piece argues these two tricks actually compete for the same space, though a bit of both can mix when features are rare enough.

simple.text: This is an informal note by Chris Olah about how neural networks store information in their neurons. It looks at "distributed representations," an old idea from neuroscience and AI meaning information is spread across many neurons instead of one neuron per thing. The author argues this term actually covers two different ideas, which the piece calls composition and superposition.

This matters because breaking a network's representations into separate, independent pieces is necessary to escape being overwhelmed by huge numbers of possible combinations, and to actually understand how networks work inside.

Composition means using separate neurons for simple features, like "green" and "square," that combine to represent objects. This uses fewer neurons, lets a network generalize what it learns about one combination to others, and stays easy to interpret. Superposition instead crams far more items into a code than there are neurons, like 4 bits representing 16 numbers, but you then lose the ability to simply read off most features.

The note argues composition and superposition compete for the same limited space, so a code can't fully have both at once. But when features are sparse, meaning most combinations never actually occur, networks can mix the two strategies, using the unused "holes" in composed space to store other features through superposition.

fuller.text: This is an informal note by Chris Olah, not a polished paper, looking at how "distributed representations" relate to a related idea called "superposition." Distributed representations spread information about something across many parts instead of using one dedicated unit. Superposition is when a network stores more separate pieces of information than it has neurons for, by overlapping them.

The piece argues this matters because breaking representations down into separate, independent pieces is necessary to escape the problem where possibilities explode as more features are added, and to truly understand how neural networks work inside.

Its key claim is that "distributed representations" actually hides two different strategies: composition, where separate features like color and shape combine to describe something, and superposition, where features overlap and share neurons. These two strategies have very different effects on how well a network can generalize and on what can be read out, and they compete for the same limited space rather than simply adding together.

Using toy examples of colored shapes, the note shows codes ranging from one neuron per combination, to separate neurons for color and shape that combine, to fully overlapped codes that pack in far more items than there are neurons but are hard to read cleanly. It also shows the two strategies can partly mix when features are sparse, meaning combinations are rare, leaving room to tuck extra features into the unused space.
